## Part A - Vectors

```{r}
scores <- c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84)
scores
subjects <- c("Math", "Science", "English", "History", "PE")
subjects

odds <- seq(1, 19, by=2)
odds
seq(0, 1, length.out = 5)

rep("A", 4)
rep(c("A", "B"), each = 2)
rep(c("A", "B"), 2)

#Q1
age <- c(15, 28, 32, 36, 27, 18, 52, 39, 42, 29, 35, 31, 27, 22, 37, 34, 19, 20, 57, 49, 50, 37, 46, 25, 17, 12, 42, 53, 41, 51, 35, 24, 33, 8)
age

#A. - There are 34 data points
length(c(age))

#B.
recip <- 1 / age
recip

#C. - It prints the vector age, then prints zero, and then prints the vector age again.
new_age <- c(age, 0, age)
new_age

#D. - Minimum age = 8, Maximum age = 57
age <- c(min(age), max(age))
age

#Q2
#The difference between each and times in rep() is how the code repeats the elements. In each, the code repeats the elements in order("A", "A", "B", "B" - A is repeated first, then followed by B) while in times, it repeats the elements alternately ("A', "B", "A", "B").

#Q3
#The arguments by and length.out has their own function. Using the by argument, it controls the step size of the code, skipping elements based on the assigned value until it reaches the end point. Meanwhile, length.out argument deals with the elements or the number of values at an assigned range. It can come off as decimals.

#Q4
#A. - vec_num
vec_num <- seq(20, 60)
vec_num

#B. mean of vec_num
mean(vec_num)

#C. - sum of vec_num
sum(vec_num)

#D. - There are 41 data points.
length(vec_num)
```

## Part B - Subsetting Vectors

```{r}
grades <- c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84)
names(grades) <- c("Math", "Science", "English", "History", "PE")

grades[3]
grades[c(1, 4)]
grades[c("Science", "PE")]

grades[-c(1, 4)]

grades[grades >= 85]

#Q5
#Since negative indexing is all about removing elements while knowing its position, it is best used when carefully removing unnecessary files that are detected clearly within a folder. For logical indexing, it is best used for determining what objects are cheap without manually scouting which one is cheaper or expensive.

#Q6
grades[10]
#It returns as [NA] instead of an error. R does this to prevent sudden crashes, and treats [NA] as an indicator that the object does not exist or needs to be assigned for it to run properly.

#Q7
Filter(function(i) { all(i %% c(3,5,7) != 0) }, seq(100))
```

## Part C - Vector Operations and append()
```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
y <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)
x + y
x * 2

z <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
short <- c(1, 0)
z + short

fruits <- c("apple", "banana", "cherry")
append(fruits, "date")
append(fruits, "kiwi", after = 1)

#Q8
#The R's "recycling rule" repeats the short vector until it becomes a long vector, so it could be even with the given longer vector and could be added together. It fits evenly since 6 is a multiple by 2, so it wouldn't cause any errors when running this code.

#Q9
z + c(1, 0, 1)
z + c(1, 0, 1, 1)
#The first one is recycled without a warning since the long vector is a multiple of the short vector. Whereas the second code receives a warning, but prints the result anyway because the long vector is not a multiple of the short vector.
```

## Part D - Lists: Creating and Subsetting
```{r}
student <- list(name = "Maria Santos", age = 20,
                grades = c(88, 92, 79), is_enrolled = TRUE)

student["grades"]
class(student["grades"])

student[["grades"]]
class(student[["grades"]])

student$name

student$grades[2]

#Q10
class(student["grades"])
class(student[["grades"]])
#The single bracket returns a result "list" as it prints the vector itself, while the double bracket is "numeric", printing out the numbers or what is inside the vector instead.

#Q11
#A vector can only hold one type of data, so the single bracket "[ ]" is enough to get a smaller vector. A list can hold different things, so R needs "[ ]" to get a smaller list and double brackets "[[ ]]" to print out the item within the vector.
```

## Part E - Critical-Thinking Challenge
```{r}
inventory <- list(
  item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"),
  price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00),
  in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

inventory$item[inventory$in_stock]

inventory$item     <- append(inventory$item, "Ruler")
inventory$price    <- append(inventory$price, 15.00)
inventory$in_stock <- append(inventory$in_stock, TRUE)

#Q12
#First, the 'inventory$in_stock' pulls out the logical vector c(TRUE TRUE FALSE). Then, the 'inventory$item' takes out the character vector c("Notebook" "Pen" "Eraser"). Using the logical vector inside [ ] keeps the elements of item where the matching position is TRUE. This works because both vectors have the same length and the same order, which means the elements are equally positioned/aligned. The list stores them separately but keeps the shared positions evenly.

#Q13
#In this situation, none of the elements are linked. If sorting or deleting elements and forgetting to include the other ones, the data gets mixed up, like "Pen" ending up with the price of "Eraser". This would disrupt the flow of the code, and would cause bugs when running it. To solve this, putting everything in one list or data frame keeps each item's details together, which could help connect the elements to their corresponding vectors. In this case, I would go for making a list or data frame.
```
## Conclusion

#Vectors hold elements of a single data type, while lists can hold a variety of elements, including vectors, matrices, and other lists. Vectors are best for simple, uniform data such as clean rows and columns of numbers. Lists are better for group-related but different elements, such as the student’s name, grades and student's ID number. When the elements are parallel columns of equal length, a data frame is best used for this next step of coding.
